projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Bernard Nutter was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: I am Bernard Nutter. I was born in Wilmington.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Do you remember where you were born in?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: 3515-1/2 Madison Street, Wilmington, Delaware, in the house.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You were born in the -- actually in the house?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: I was born in the house. Wasn't born in a hospital.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How about this one?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: I don't know about him, frankly.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: He was born in the house or hospital?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: We all were. I was, too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: My dad and uncle were, too.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: We had a midwife. It was grandma, wasn't it? My grandma was the midwife.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Sir, this is one thing you cannot --

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And while he's speaking, you can be thinking about -- I am going to be actually going and doing the same type of interview. You can just let me know who you are. And when I ask the question, you don't answer the question. You say -- if I say, What is your name, you go, My name is --

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you repeat everything I say. Because you are not going to hear me on the camera at all. This is just going to be you guys.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Are we ready? He is. Let's just do a quick review. I am --

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: I am Bernard Nutter, Senior. I better put that in there because my boy is Bernard. I am Bernard Nutter, Senior. I was born in Wilmington, Delaware on Madison Street. I went to 23 School, Warner School and Brown Vocational Tech. I graduated in 1942 in June and went into the service in November of '42. I joined the United States Marine Corps. I was not drafted.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Now, so now, let's go back to -- let's go back to December 7. You don't remember it too well. But let's talk from December 7 on. You were still in school?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: I was still in school, yeah. I was in the summer. December 7, the attack on Pearl Harbor, I was still in school at Brown Vocational. It was quite a thing in the school. I think it instrumented me in joining the Marine Corps.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. So let's now talk about you went into the Marine Corps in Wilmington or whatever. And talk about where you went. I mean, you went for basic training: I went for basic training here. After basic training, I went to maybe gun school or whatever you went to.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: That's exactly what I did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And then from there, we were going to be assigned to whatever Marines on the Independence frigate in Philadelphia.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Right. Right. Okay. I joined the Marine Corps, and I was shipped to Parris Island, South Carolina. After that, we were segregated due to our education. And I moved to Norfolk Navy Yard and the gunnery school. I was a marine gunner, operating 40 millimeters as fire control. On graduation from there, I was reassigned to the Philadelphia Navy yard aboard the USS Independence CVL. I was outfitted from the New York ship to the Philadelphia Navy yard. And we took on our 40 millimeters, and I was trained on the 40-millimeter Mark 14 sight. We took a shakedown to Trinidad. And on the way down, we took target practice. And I learned how to operate the new sight. Upon return to the Philadelphia Navy yard after our shakedown, we were outfitted with -- we did away with the 50-caliber machine guns and remounted 20-millimeter machine guns. We had a battery of -- on the starboard side forward, we had a battery of 20s. And I was on mount 7 with fire control on 40 millimeters. After we were outfitted in Philadelphia, we went south to the Panama Canal. Went over to San Diego, California and were outfitted with the F-4 Rummons (ph). From there, we took a shakedown -- speed shakedown to San Francisco, California. And we transferred our F-4s off at Mare (ph) Island, California to the F-6s, which were heavily armed with machine guns and rockets and faster than the F4. From there, we went to the Hawaiian Islands, Pearl Harbor. The ships were still a smaller link, so to speak, and in the harbor there. And we went to what we call Ford Island. That's an air base opposite of Pearl Harbor. From there we went out and we went to the Pacific. And our first strike was on Marcus Island, 600-some miles from Japan. We were hoping to keep the Japs from coming in through the Aleutians and Marcus Island to the Americans, because they were that close. From there we went south, and we operated out of a place called Eniwetok. And we went into the first battle. We were in -- it was the Philippine Sea, where our sister ship, the Princeton, was sunk and several other heavy ships. From there, we moved up on to Tarawa, where we were torpedoed. We were then towed back to an island called Funafuti, where they outfitted us with a patch on our ship and we were towed back to Hunters Point, California. We were repaired there. And from there, we were shipped back out again. That's the good old Marine Corps system, in again out again. From there, we went over to the Philippines. We hit Manila. We hit Luzon. And we moved north to Okinawa where we shot down quite a few planes. According to the scriptures on the side of our ship, we shot over 100 planes down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, you weren't involved with Midway?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: We were involved with Midway later. We were laying off of Midway, north of Midway. And the Japs came in, and we had to battle the first battle of Midway. And then we come back. And we operated out of the Philippine Sea, South China Sea. And we went down to the South China Sea and bombarded French Indo-China. From there, we went back north. Because through the Ballentine (ph) Straits, the Japs were coming in that way. And Nimitz moved down to meet them. And I was on a battle station, 3 and 5. We had -- we had a different admiral. We had Spruance, and they had Nimitz.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: About Halsey?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Halsey came later. Halsey came later, and he took over the Third and the Fifth fleet. Operating with Halsey was quite different than operating with Spruance. Spruance was a tactician. Halsey was -- his nickname was Bull Halsey because he just went in like a bull and regardless of who got hit or not. We shot down quite a few planes there. And like I say, we had some hits. Luckily we had a wooden deck on our carriers. The English operated with us. And they were different. They had, their ships were metal decks. And when they got hit, why everything went right through. From there we went up to Okinawa, off Okinawa. We missed Iwo Jima due to the fact that we were shipping south to get supplies and get aircraft. We missed Iwo Jima. But our next shot, we went into Japan and got the Marines off the ships of the Third and Fifth fleets who were the first provisional marine landing course of the Sixth Division. And I was with the group that occupied Yokosuka.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, was that after the bomb?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: That was before the bomb.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Okay. Let's -- let me just -- just -- so just -- now, you know, Spruance --

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- married a lady from here?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: He's from Delaware, and he married a lady from out in Greenville; Centreville, Greenville area. Yes, I did know that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Because Halsey, his grandson, I guess, used to be with Wilmington Trust?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: He retired a few years ago. He also had a -- was Nimitz from here?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Not that I know of. He might have.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Spruance was from?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Spruance was from here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Spruance, there was two sides of Spruance. General Spruance?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: We had Admiral.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You had Admiral Spruance?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: That whole gang. Yeah; yeah. And Michener is another one. We had an Admiral Michener that came in at the Battle of Philippines. He was on our ship. We were a flag at that time, what they call a flag ship, because that's --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you ever run into anybody -- I mean, did anybody on board from Delaware?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We had a -- I had -- trying to find a picture for you. We had a group of us had a circle of -- they were -- I was the only marine from Delaware. The rest of them were sailors. We had gunners, and we had different types.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That would be interesting to see if any of those guys are -- do you know if any of those guys are still around?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: The only one I know lives by me, and I can get in touch with him, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: But he actually was with you?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Oh, yeah; yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That would be good. Remind me. I have to ask you about some of that stuff, too. Okay. So now we have gone to Japan. So actually, explain about Japan occupied before you know like approximately what date and then the bomb came later or something.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Datewise, it is kind of hard to remember. But we went into the Yokosuka naval base and we occupied the former Japanese barracks. Might sound funny, but they were the cleanest military people I have ever met. We could eat off the floor in those barracks they had. That's how they were. Of course they were regimented. Everybody knows that. And we occupied that area, and we patrolled the streets. People were more or less afraid of us from the previous propaganda they put out about us about the Marines, what we would do. Of course we didn't. But as we were there for a while, they became more friendly and we went into the towns of Tokyo and the different towns we went around on liberty after we were --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Just to digress a second, which I think is timely is, why did it work there versus -- I know stuff happened later. But why did it work there when you took that town over versus what's going on over in Iraq right now?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Well, if we would have met the military like they are meeting, then probably would have been a little different because the kamikaze attitude of the Japanese soldier and sailors and so forth. But we were meeting civilians. And I think, in my opinion, that they were more or less, how would I put it, programmed to treat us right or we might retaliate. I think they were more or less were more fearful than they were --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Well, Pascal (ph), was actually embedded over in Iraq?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: But what he says that is very interesting is the country is really made up of three different groups. So it is actually probably Japan just because of their nature, was one big --

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Well, they are mostly (Shinto), I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: As far as I know. I am not that up on the history of their division.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Let's talk about kamikazes. How many of those did you run into or if you did?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Well, off Okinawa was the first time we were embedded with kamikazes. If you look at the pictures I gave you, you will see that their kamikazes, they are not just ordinary fighters coming in. Kamikazes would come in in a group. This is affecting me and my group. And our lookouts would spot them. Of course, we had radar. That was one of the good things we had on our ship. We'd spot a group coming in. And, of course, we would keep an eye out for them. But once they broke formation --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Hold on.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Yeah, the kamikaze would come in in a group and they would fly real high. And they would break formation. And they'd try to come after the carriers because that was the detriment to them. Because our ships were up looking for them and so forth. And it was quite an experience to see one of them coming at you. And our particular group shot down quite a few of them. Once they headed for you, they didn't turn around. You had to knock them down or they'd hit you. We took -- I was going to say, we took a hit on a foxhole where the quad 40s were and put that out of service one of the kamikazes hit us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How many did that take out of the plan?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: That didn't take anybody out, but the torpedoes that I told you about earlier took out quite a few of us, 60 or 100 guys. But as far as kamikazes, they didn't affect us as far as killing anybody. They just put our forward guns out of service. They concentrated on what's called the foxhole.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. So let's go back to Japan. We have now landed in Japan. We are in Yokosuka?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Yeah, Yokosuka.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Well, we landed there, of course. And we organized in the Japanese barracks, the ones I told you about previously. And we patrolled the areas around and we went looking for people who would be similar to a kamikaze but were land-based people who tried to snipe at us and so forth. And we cleaned them up pretty good. The Fourth Division I -- don't quote me exactly on the Fourth -- it was either the Fourth or Sixth Division ground Marines took over Yokohama and (?Mary's Lake?). They had cleaned out the pockets, and it was pretty peaceful from thereon.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How soon after did they drop the big bomb?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: That you'd have to look up in the history. We were not in Japan at the time they dropped the bomb.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: But you went into -- you went into Japan?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You just say it was six months later they dropped the bomb or a year?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Six months to a year, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, ok.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Because we were pulled out and the regular ground pounder Marines went in and took over. And the fleet Marines, which I belonged to, came out, and we went aboard our ship. And then, of course, we reformed our fleets.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tell me a little bit about fleet Marines, about how the difference between, you know, the regular ground pounders or grunts versus the details or the --

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Well, we take the exact same training as the --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Let's start again. Tell me, the marine -- is it a marine? What's it called, marine service?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Marine?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: USSMA. That's United States Seagone Marine Association.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Well, let's start from scratch and give you an idea. When you go to boot camp, you are just a boot camp marine. You are not anything else. Then they take your education and take your basic training background and they send you to school. That's when I was sent to sea school and gunnery school. Okay. The ground Marines are sent to Quantico or some other place like that, California or something like that. Their training is more intense on the rifles. And we were more intense on our antiaircraft and guns of that nature. We were also trained with rifles, but that was secondary. They had a hell of a life. I mean, they lived in the mud. And we lived aboard ship and ate like sailors. We had good food. We had good, clean bunks and so forth. They lived the hell life. I mean, if you were a ground pounder, you were in trouble.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Other Marines, they don't have -- they just basically -- they basically have a small group of Marines on board these ships now?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Yes. Yes. We had about 75 Marines. We were a gunnery crew. And we were also as the Navy called us, the military police of the ships. We guarded the brig. If the sailors went off ship and got in trouble, they brought them back. Instead of putting them in a civilian jail, they put them in our jail. And, of course, depending on what your specialty was, you guarded the prison. And it was way down in the bottoms of the ship. But basically we were the -- we were the marine police, if you want to put it that way, of the ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Our primary job was gunnery.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. So when we -- okay. So let's talk about that. After you finish Japan, you went back to sea and then how did you get out of the war?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Okay. We -- I was aboard the Independence, and we went to Portland, Oregon. From there -- not Portland, Oregon. Yeah, that's right. Portland, Oregon we were decommissioned. And I went from there to Bremerton, Washington. And we were discharged in Bremerton, Washington. And I took a troop train across the United States to Bainbridge, Maryland. At that time, it was a naval base. And they discharged us at Bainbridge, Maryland. And my older brother, Walter, came and picked me up and brought me home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How -- was that right at war's end?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Yes, it was. Well, it was 1945 in November. So.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That was after Japan?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: After Japan had surrendered.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right. So where were you when Japan -- when they had the truce?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: When they did the truce?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: There were two dates, August the 15th? Yeah, August.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: '45 was the --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What they called the VE Day?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: VJ?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: VJ, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: But the actual documents were signed aboard the Missouri the 2nd of September. So where were you guys around there? (20 MINUTES)

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Okay. We were laying off Japan. And the third fleet was still there. And then after the signing and all, they started to disburse different ships. And we were one of the few that was out there the longest, you know. So we were the first one to be shipped back. We -- of course, we stopped at Pearl along the way over. And after Pearl, we went into and I was discharged from Bremerton, Washington.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, were you married at the time?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: No, I was single.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Just out of high school. I had enough problems without being married.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. So now, okay, so let's -- now, when they dropped the bombs, I mean, did you know about that? Did you find out about that?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: We found out through the naval correspondence. We had a ships paper and we found out that way.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So did you know that day it happened or --

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: No, a few days later. Because --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So nobody knew it was going to go on?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Nobody had the slightest idea?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: All right. So then you came back. So let's do a little bit, you came back to Wilmington?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Came back to Wilmington. I went to work as a plumber's helper. Because I learned plumbing in Brown vocational. And I worked there until I got an inkling through being in the Marine Corps, we were more or less like police. So I joined the Wilmington police force.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Where did you work up there? What company did you work for? Not Rescovich (ph)?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: No. No. He wasn't even around then. I will tell you in a minute. Gothrup (ph) Brothers. Gothrup Brothers was on Orange Street at 8th. It is a bowling alley there now. But that was their building. I don't know if it is a bowling alley now or not.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That's where John Lyons had his studio?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Exactly. He was on the first deck -- first floor. Sorry about that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And the bowling alley upstairs, that was actually the --

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Grady's (ph) Alley?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Grady's Alley, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Do you remember that fire they had?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: We took out the whole -- if you can visualize, the building had an archway. We go through that arch and everything of that -- left of the arch all of the way back was Gothrup's. And then I went on to the police force.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You went on to where the police force?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Wilmington Police Force. And due to my background -- I forgot to tell you about this. I guess it is all right to slip it in. But I picked up photography aboard ship. Because I knew some of the guys aboard ship. And I used to sneak back in the off time in the photo lab to develop and do pictures. So I got an inkling for that. So when I joined the police force, they moved me off the street to the records and identification division. And I was working for a Captain Brian. And I worked there for, I was on the police force 3-1/2 years. And due to my plugging around the city, I found out that there was a more lucrative job at Dupont Company, and I went to work for Dupont and stayed there 20 years.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Let's talk -- I am going to slip this in. Is that okay? Did -- your other brothers, your oldest brother was a civilian?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Yeah, my oldest brother was a technician at Westoverfield in Massachusetts. He was not a military person. My middle brother, Bill, I think you know him, he was in the United States Air Force over in Europe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right. That was it?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: There's only three of us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. So during the war while the war was on, were you worried about Bill?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Or was Bill worried about you?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Well, I was going to say Bill was the worry wart. Because I didn't have time to worry. I was scared. Bill used to send us V mail, was it called? It was the little gizmos we used to get. And he would send that to me, and I would send one back to him. And we were corresponding that way. But he would send it in June and I'd probably get it in December by the time we got to a place where we could get mail. But it was interesting. We could only write certain things. But like being brothers, why he could read between the lines, and I could read between his lines, you know what I mean. But we kept in touch with each other. Now, my brother, Bill, before he went overseas he was with my oldest brother, Walter, and then, of course, I don't know what he did between him and Walter during the war because I was too busy ducking.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. He was the hero or you were the hero?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Bill is the hero. (25 Minutes)

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: I just went over there and did my job.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: All right. How do you want to do this, together? Yeah. Let's talk about the living conditions aboard and when you were at battle stations, how tedious that was maybe. And did you lose any gunners? I mean, did you lose any guys that were there?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Okay. You want me to talk now?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah, go ahead.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Well, as far as food is concerned, the Navy puts out good food, when we can get it. Now, we got into what we call a combat area. You ate what was aboard supplies. And then from there on in, we even went to K rations we were so engrossed in combat off Okinawa. That's where the kamikazes were keeping us busy, you know. So we went down to that. But other than that, the food was good. Our racks, or bunks, as you call them --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You can say racks.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: We were close to our gun stations. In other words, when GQ or torpedo of defense came up, we could get there in less than three or four minutes because we didn't have to go very far. We just left quarters and run up the ladders and went on to the gun posts. The biggest thing we had trouble with was our evaporators. To explain what an evaporator is, that's taking saltwater and making drinking water out of it. And our evaporators went kaput. So we had a problem there. But if you have ever taken a saltwater shower, you will never forget it. But that's quite a --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That was part of the drinking water?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Drinking wasn't bad. You could still get a salty -- the drinking water wasn't bad once they got the evaporators, you know, working. But still, you could tell it was not pure water because it had like a foreign taste to it. But other than that, food and everything was good. Sacks were good. We did our own laundry. That's something that a lot of people probably don't understand. The Navy has a laundry aboard ship. And the Marines did their own laundry. We went on down to the laundry, washed the clothes, put them through the presses, and all and pressed our own clothes and brought them back. The Navy made room for us to do that. Obviously, they didn't want to do it. So we did it. But living conditions were comparatively good. I mean, compared to guys on the beach. The only thing that was bad about it was there was a heck of a lot of war out there. If they got to you, you had to learn how to swim. And, of course, we lost at the torpedoing, we lost, don't quote me exactly, but eight to ten guys. When the torpedo hit, it took a gun tub, if you are familiar with what that is, and flipped it across the deck. And one guy actually jumped off the gun tub as it was going across the deck. But he died later from the concussion and all that. And the hole in our ship was 80 by 60, roughly. You could drive a truck through it. In fact, two of the shafts on our four shafts, that's why we had to be towed. And watertight doors saved the ship. I got pictures of it, if you are interested, in what a ship looked like after it was torpedoed. Because it took about a 30 or some degree list. And if we'd have went a couple of degrees more, we'd have capsized. But we didn't because of the fact we had good, watertight doors. So other than that, why --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How long were you at your gun stations when you were in battle? How involved was that?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Well, that's a good question. Well, if you went to -- well, first of all, I will give you torpedo defense. _____??, that's an acronym for submarines. Because when you go to torpedo defense, either the cans or the -- just other ships picked up a sound, and we went to torpedo defense. What we were going to do with torpedo defense, I don't know, because we had antiaircraft guns. And I don't know what the heck we were going to use them for, but we were there anyways. General quarters, everybody comes up. The gunners go on torpedo defense. On general quarters, we all went up. And that could be anything from a ship, an airplane or an OKA (ph) bomb. Are you familiar with them?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: That's where a bomb that the Japanese get inside of and fly it to their destination and blow the bomb and whatever they are coming at. We didn't get hit with it, but Franklin, you probably heard of that, it was off our starboard quarter, he got hit with two OKA bombs, however you pronounce it, and with other things. That was quite a sight. But they still went back to New York and to be reoutfitted. They didn't sink. They didn't sink them, but they took a hell of a wallop.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, at your typical Okinawa, how long were you at battle stations and stuff? During the battle, how long when they were all coming at you?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Well, we sounded GQ roughly 0400. And you stayed on GQ until the flag up top would tell us we were secured. I have been on them from daylight to daylight and never got off. We slept in the tubs. So depends on where you were, how bad the enemy was, and so forth. But other than that, why maybe six or seven hours.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How intense were these planes coming in at you?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: They come in squads. And what I told you earlier, when they come in, they peeled off. And the main targets at that time were carriers. They tried to get us because we were a deck command. And the battle ships couldn't go after them, but our guys could go after them with our planes. But due to radar, we knew they were coming and we launched. And, of course, the boys in the airplanes, they did a good job, too. But general quarters would generally last, I'd say, six to eight hours. Mostly daylight. The Japs didn't do much flying at night. We were the first night fighter carrier out there. And it was -- we had airplanes that could fly at night because they had radar in their wings.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: F-6s?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: F-6s.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: F-6, I mean.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. We did away with the F4s in Lamayo, California and went to F6s. But the F6s had a big ball in the right wing. Because our wings folded up. And they had a big ball in the right wing, and that's what it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So when they come in in these swarms, how long did that last?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Until every one of them got shot down, because they never returned. They didn't go back. They just kept coming in, coming in. They went after different ships. And as -- I can show you in some of the pictures.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Hours?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: It could be a couple of hours anyway. Depending on the intensity of the gunners.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was that intense for you?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Can I tell you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. I want you to tell me.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Well, let me tell you, it is not fun. Everybody will tell you they weren't scared, but they are liars. Because you shit razor blades when they start coming at you. And you just hope that you get them. I mean, of course, I was intense inside that sight. The only thing I saw was what I was shooting at. But they come after you, it is -- there's nobody can tell me they weren't scared. But you did your job. You know, I think it is just, I don't know what the medical word would be, but you just do it because you are scared if you don't do it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You probably get like, you know, with firefighting and stuff. When you are thinking about it when you are there, it is different when you step back afterwards?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Exactly. Exactly. When you are in flighting the fire, you don't think of what you are doing. You know what you are supposed to do. Same thing with gunnery. When they give you the word to open fire, then you are so intense on doing what you are doing, that you don't have time. Actually, you don't have time to get scared until it is all over. Then, like I say, the word I used before.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Then you are scared for the next time you are going out?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Right. You know what is going to happen. The first one is tough. After that, it is routine. You are just routinely scared. You are just hoping that they don't get you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: But it is bad when your buddies get it. Because -- like I say, those guys on the starboard side, they were coming after us. It was our gun tub they were after. Because we were pretty active. But they ended up dropping a fish in the starboard side aft and those guys got it still.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What did they drop it out of?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: A Betty. Okay. I will explain that to our. Betty is a similar airplane to -- ours is probably copied off of it. But a Betty is a four- engine bomber that has a bay that opens up. And they come in low. They come in low. In fact, they are almost the props hitting the water. That's how low they come in. They drop their fish. And what we knew what they were going to do -- can I use my hands -- we knew they were going to do it once they dropped it. We knew they were going to come up. And that's when we opened up at them. And you can knock them apart. (35 MINUTES 35 SECONDS) So we had a pattern we shot. We shot a pattern of right, left, top and bottom. And keep them in the middle. That was my job keeping them in the middle with my sight. And once our projectiles got out there and proximity fuses went off, then boom, they were gone.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah. Okay. How much -- well, how deep did the radar penetrate? How much warning time did you have?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: Roughly, I am going to give you a guess, but roughly 50, 40, 50 miles.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: The radar was only good?

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: The radar was only good to roughly 50 miles. And as they come in, of course, the -- we call them bogies. As the bogies come in, why they got bigger and they could more or less know what was good on. But they come in as a regular blip. And as they come in, then the radar guys in the high sea could tell what kind of planes they were by the shape and so forth and so on. They were well versed on that. They wouldn't tell us Bettys, but fighters. They wouldn't say Bettys. They'd say bombers, fighters, so forth. But they -- basically the radar men saved our butt because we knew they were coming.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Good. All right.

sp.speaker: Bernard Nutter
sp.p: I can stand down now? (END)
